column6: Moses recalls Israel standing before a mountain of fire, cloud, and thick darkness; this is a specific Sinai setting beside the commentary's account of Moses and Israel confronting the limits of divine sight.
At Horeb Israel hears God's voice from the fire but sees no form; this makes the commentary's pairing of recited sound and restricted vision an explicit feature of the same revelation scene.
Moses repeats that Israel saw no form and therefore must not make an image; beside Q 7:143, this gives a distinct scriptural consequence of a theophany without visible form.

While the people stand at a distance, Moses approaches the thick darkness where God is; this makes hiddenness the setting of direct encounter, complementing the commentary's open/hidden knowledge pair.
The people hide their counsel in darkness and ask who sees them; this is a direct prophetic example of the concealment the commentary says cannot remove anything from divine knowledge.
The psalm asks whether the one who planted the ear cannot hear and the one who formed the eye cannot see; this joins the commentary's audible and visual forms of cehr to their divine source.
The psalm says YHWH knows human thoughts; this gives a concise counterpart to the commentary's hidden contents remaining known even when not voiced.
Hannah's song says YHWH is a God of knowledge who weighs actions; after her silent prayer, this connects the commentary's prayer scene to divine knowledge and judgment.

column5: elders think God does not see
column6: In Ezekiel's vision, elders worship in hidden rooms and say YHWH does not see them; the scene supplies a concrete false belief that the commentary's open/hidden knowledge claim overturns.

column5: God knows what comes to mind
column6: YHWH says He knows what comes into the people's minds; this is a direct counterpart to the commentary's unspoken contents of the heart being within divine knowledge.
Ecclesiastes says God brings every work, including every hidden thing, into judgment; this extends the commentary's claim that hidden matters remain known to a concrete judgment scene.
A book of remembrance is written before YHWH for those who fear His name; this joins the commentary's linked themes of divine memory, recorded words, and the name invoked in worship.

column5: no one can hide from God
column6: Sirach challenges the person who thinks they can be hidden from the Lord among the crowd; this gives a distinct wisdom-text setting for the commentary's claim that no concealed thing escapes divine awareness.

column5: secret almsgiving seen by the Father
column6: Jesus says the Father sees charitable giving done in secret; this extends the commentary's open/hidden pair from prayer and recitation to a specific concealed ethical action.
Jesus says what is covered will be revealed and what is hidden will be known; this is a direct continuation of the commentary's claim that hiddenness does not mean disappearance from knowledge.
Jesus says people will answer for every careless word; this applies the commentary's claim about God's knowledge of speech to words that speakers might treat as unimportant.

column5: Spirit supplies the persecuted speaker's words
column6: Jesus tells disciples not to prepare their defense because the Holy Spirit will give them what to say; this is a Christian counterpart to the commentary's insistence that prophetic speech is given rather than owned.

Peter says prophecy did not arise from human will, but people spoke from God as carried by the Holy Spirit; this directly parallels the commentary's claim that the messenger does not possess the source of recitation.

column5: God judges human secrets through Christ
column6: Paul says God judges people's secrets through Christ; this gives a Christian judgment formulation for the hidden contents that the commentary says God knows.
Christ says He searches minds and hearts and repays each according to deeds; this joins inward knowledge to judgment, as the commentary's account of hidden matters does.
John sees the dead judged from opened books according to their deeds; this gives an apocalyptic record-and-disclosure counterpart to the commentary's claim that God counts what people forget.

At the temple dedication Solomon says YHWH has chosen to dwell in thick darkness; this supplies a distinct biblical way to pair God's presence with concealment beside the commentary's manifest/hidden knowledge.

Isaiah calls YHWH the God who hides Himself and Israel's Savior; this adds a biblical theme of divine hiddenness to the commentary's distinction between God being hidden from human sight and knowing what is hidden.
God gives Moses His name as a memorial through generations; this complements the commentary's claim that the divine name at the ayah's hinge belongs to worship and remembrance, not impersonal fate.

column5: Israel's confession of the one YHWH
column6: The Shema names YHWH as Israel's one God; beside the commentary's emphasis on Allah's name at the exception clause, this gives a central Jewish liturgical confession to read alongside al-Fatiha.

column5: love YHWH with the whole heart
column6: The Shema immediately commands love of YHWH with all heart, soul, and strength; this concretely joins the divine name to worshipful devotion as the commentary does.

column5: stones as a sign for future questions
column6: Joshua sets stones as a sign so children will ask what they mean; this gives a concrete human use of visible markers beside the commentary's claim that God's knowledge does not need a sign.
The stones are to be a memorial for Israel; this shows a community using a visible sign to preserve memory, contrasting with the commentary's divine knowledge that needs no landmark.

The Mishnah says all is foreseen while freedom is granted; this is a specific Jewish formulation of the tension between divine knowing and human willing that the commentary resolves through God's will.

column5: all is in Heaven's hands except awe of Heaven
column6: The Talmud places everything in Heaven's hands except reverence of Heaven; this gives a rabbinic boundary to divine sovereignty beside the commentary's claim that human plans and memory remain dependent on God's will.

column5: God works both willing and doing
column6: Paul says God is at work in believers both to will and to act; this closely parallels the commentary's claim that even human willing depends on God.

column5: Peter remembers after Jesus looks at him
column6: After the rooster, Jesus looks at Peter and Peter remembers Jesus' prediction; this gives a narrative instance of a forgotten word returning when the commentary says remembering follows forgetting.
